s12i.slug: TUESDAY · 11:22 PM · THE MOONWALK — AN INDEX CARD
body: The fog has come up off the river. It started as a gray skin low on the black water, and now it has climbed the rocks and the wooden steps and put a ring around the lamp at the top of them, and Algiers is gone, lamps, landing, levee and all, erased. The cold has got into the wet wood under him and is working up. Behind them the Quarter hasn’t heard about any fog. It roars on.

Lena hasn’t moved since she stopped on *For —*. She sits facing him inside the Carhartt between his knees, the tin a hard corner at her collarbone, her palm on his chest where it came to rest, and she looks hard at the third button of his shirt.
“The dinner,” she says at last. “I told you we’d get to the dinner.”
He waits.

“Julian is good.” She says it to the button first, and then she lifts her head and says it to him, because that seems to be the rule tonight. “He’s good, Jack. He’s the kindest man I know, and the most patient, and Lord knows I’ve tested it — I’ve tested that man like a seawall. He doesn’t believe one thing I believe. Not one. And some weeks he lives it better than I do. He’d hate me for saying that, so I never have. I’m saying it to you.”
Her palm presses on his chest.
“I was going to end it after Christmas.”
The band on Decatur has gone quiet. In the gap he can hear a woman somewhere on the square laughing at something, on and on.
“For you,” Lena says.
Nothing on the end of it. She puts it there between his shirt and her hand and leaves it.

“I decided at home. On Mama’s back steps, in my coat, after we’d hung up one night — I don’t even know which night anymore, they all ran together into one long night with snow on your end. I’d sit out there after with the phone going cold in my hand and think, that’s the person I tell things to. And if that’s the person I tell things to, then I owe Julian a true thing. So I wrote it down.” Her mouth goes crooked. “You know me. I don’t trust my face with anything I mean. An index card, in capitals, so my hand wouldn’t shake on it. For the dinner — his birthday dinner, the Monday after. After Hale. Two days late, because he’d been home for it.”
She looks off into the fog where Algiers used to be.

“I had it in my pocket at that seminar. All through Dido. I had it in my pocket while you sat at the other end of that table and didn’t look at me. And Sunday night I’d seen what I’d seen.” She doesn’t say what. She told him an hour ago: the status, the gate, Laney taking the laptop. “So Monday I sat across from him at a table with a candle on it, with that card in my coat, and I didn’t use it. I let him order for me. I let him take a picture.”
“I saw the picture.”
“I know you did,” she says. “That’s why I let him take it.”
He remembers it, in 412, on a Tuesday morning, on a screen: *birthday dinner, two days late*, and her name on it.
“Fury,” Lena says. “And pride. Two of the seven at one table, and I didn’t even get dessert.”
Her fingers close in his shirt.
“I made a good man a guardrail, Jack. I did exactly what you did with Becca, and I called *you* names for it.”
He starts to say something. He doesn’t know yet what.
“And it’s not the same,” she says. “You know it’s not the same. I never —”
She stops. Her mouth stays open on the next word, and then it closes over it. He doesn’t need the word. It’s the one nobody is saying out here tonight, and she won’t spend it even on a *never*.
“Is it still —”
“In my wallet.” Her free hand goes back to the hip pocket of her jeans and lies flat over it and doesn’t take anything out. “It’s his. He reads it first.”
He will never know what it says. That seems right to him, and he’s surprised how right.
“Sunday,” she says. “After Mass. To his face, when we’re both back.” And then, to the fog: “Five weeks and a day. It’s been in my wallet five weeks and a day.”

One index card. One sentence on a phone, in his father’s garage, with the space heater ticking and the snow coming down past the window in the side door. That’s all it would have taken. Any night since Christmas. Any night before it.
“If I’d said it on the phone,” he says. “Any one of those nights.”
“If I had said what *fix it* meant.”
“If I’d said, I don’t have a thing, Lena. I’ll be by the phone.”
“If I had told you on the back steps instead of telling a card.”
“If I’d told you on the stairs at All Souls that I was waiting.”
“If I had asked you what for.”

They go on a little longer, quietly, and every one of them starts the same way. Nobody hands anybody a *you*. It’s like the line on the Broussards’ shed, four and a half feet up the boards, where you can see exactly how high it came, and know exactly how little it would have taken to keep it out, and not be able to make it not have come.

body.text: “You told my brother to tell her the truth before the parade,” Lena says.
“I missed the parade.”
“You missed every one,” she says.
“You told a ninety-one-year-old woman you wished you could say what you mean.”
“She said something to you. Vy wouldn’t translate.”
“I know what she said.”
“You don’t speak Vietnamese.”
“I didn’t need to.”

body: “Father Hébert said Wednesday’s coming.”
“It’s coming in an hour.”

body.text: “On Esplanade you said you wanted me here,” he says. “Since September. And in the van you said *I did*, and I didn’t say anything back.”
body.else: “On Esplanade you said you wanted me here,” he says. “Since September. And I didn’t say anything back.”

body: “I know,” she says. “I was listening for it.”
So he says it now, the thing he kept under the oak with her fingers coming loose from his button. It isn’t the word. He doesn’t need the word for it.
“Me too. Since the porch. Since before you told me your name.”
Her hand on his chest closes, slowly, and takes a fold of his shirt with it.

Out in the fog something is pushing upriver, a long way out — a towboat, nothing of it but two smeared lights, red and green, and the low work of an engine he feels more than hears. It goes by and is gone. A minute after, its wash finds the steps. The black water lifts under them and slaps the rocks, and sucks back, and slaps again, three times, four — the only sound the river has made all night — and then it’s flat and quiet and going by again.
Lena draws back far enough to see him.
“Plain, Jack,” she says. “From now on. Even when it’s ugly. *Especially* then.”
“Plain.”

response: “Plain,” he says. “I promise.”
“I know you do.” She looks at him a long time from inside the coat, with the fog in her hair beading on every strand. “That’s what scares me about you.”

choices.text: “Then here’s the first one: I should have said it on that roof.”
response: “Then here’s the first one,” he says. “I should have said it on that roof.”
“Yes,” she says. “You should have.” Her fist in his shirt doesn’t loosen. “And I should have let you.”
Whatever it was, the end of it is still back in December, at the dash, with a van coming. He doesn’t reach for it now, and she doesn’t.
“Plain,” he says. “Like Ohio.”
“Ohio isn’t plain,” Lena says, into his collar. “It’s *beige*.” But her hand stays where it is on his chest, and after a moment it pats him there twice, like a woman testing whether a melon is ready.

s12j.slug: TUESDAY · 11:30 PM · THE MOONWALK, UNDER THE LAMP — THE TIN
body: The lamp at the head of the steps hangs in the fog with a pale wheel around it, and the light that comes down through the wheel is soft and wet and lands on her hair, and on his hands, and on the step between his boots.

He has to reach in under her chin for it. It’s been against her all night at the collarbone, a corner she found in the first minute at the rail and touched through the canvas and left alone. He works his hand into the breast pocket of the Carhartt, and she leans back to let him, and he brings it out warm from the two of them.
“You said if there was one more,” he says, “you’d know.”
He puts it in her hands.

Her thumbs know it before she looks at it. They go over the lid in the dark — the soft corners, the hinge, the letters — and stop on the first R, where his thumb has worn the paint down to bare tin from two months of riding on it. She looks at that a while.
“At the coffee cart,” she says. “With my finger on the lid. I said it to make you laugh.”
“I didn’t laugh.”
“No. You put it in your pocket like I’d handed you a finger bone of Saint Somebody in a glass box.”

“It went to Youngstown,” he says. “It sat on the workbench in my dad’s garage every night I called you, next to the space heater. It went to Christmas Mass. It came back on the plane. It rode across Texas in this pocket while you weren’t speaking to me.”
“Stop it.” Her thumb is on the lid. “I am not going to cry over an Altoids tin on a levee in front of Algiers.”
“Algiers is gone.”
“Then in front of the fog.”
She sets it on her knee, inside the coat, and he keeps his arm around her, and she opens it under the lamp.

The smell comes up first: sweet and stale and shut-in, Christmas in a pocket. Her eleven are there, packed tight, each on its slip in her capitals, and No. 1 on its curl of receipt paper from a soup restaurant in Buellton.

body.text: And on top of hers, fitted in close, six more. Six Reds, each on a strip of yellow paper torn along the blue lines, in a hand that isn’t hers: small and slanting and pressed hard into the paper, a hand no teacher ever got anywhere with.
She takes one out by its corner and tips it to the lamp.
*No. 13 · 1/20/10 · Delgado east stairwell, 3:40 a.m. · after the Fishbowl*
She puts it back on its Red exactly where it was and takes out another.
*No. 15 · 1/27/10 · Hale’s deck, 7:37 p.m. · after Hale’s*

That one she holds longer. Somewhere back in the Quarter the band on Decatur has found its feet again and is going through something with a trombone in it. She puts No. 15 back and takes out the last one, the one on top.
*No. 17 · 2/5/10 · El Paso, under the air pump, 11:55 p.m. · after the drive*
“El Paso,” she says. “Where was I?”
“In the van. Asleep.”
“I wasn’t asleep.”

He can see the van at the pump: the dome light off, her shape against the far window with her face turned to the glass. He’d stood under the air pump with his back to it so he wouldn’t have to find out whether she was watching.

The rest she reads where they lie, tipping the tin to the light, and her lips move on them the way they move at the back of Holy Rosary on a decade when she thinks she’s alone: the number, the date, the place, what it came after. He watches her read the stairwell, and Sully’s, and the curb. He watches her get to the drive.
There’s nothing on top of them. He had nothing to put in. She lifts the slips with one fingernail and looks under them anyway, all the way to the bottom of the tin.
“When did you write these?”
“Last night. In the attic, by the streetlight.” He tips his head at the yellow. “Off the bottom of Hale’s pad.”
“You tore up Hale’s essay for me.”
“I tore off the bottom. The essay’s at the top.”
“There’s one sentence at the top, Jack.”
“It’s a good sentence.”
“It *is* a good sentence.” She says it to the tin, not to him, and for a little while she doesn’t say anything else, and the fog comes and goes around the lamp.

body: “How many, Jack?”

body.text: “Six.”
She looks at the yellow over the white a long time.
body.else: She looks up at him from the tin, and down at her eleven, by themselves.

body.text: “Every one of these is me,” she says.

She runs a fingernail down the yellow strips, down the ends of them, where the last words are. “Sully’s. The Fishbowl. The curb. Hale’s. Hollis. The drive.” She reads them off in order. “There isn’t one in here that’s her.”
“No.”
“Not one.”
“With her I never wanted one.”
Lena takes that in with her eyes on the tin. “I don’t know if I’m supposed to be flattered or insulted.”
“Both.”
“Both,” she agrees, to the lid.

She takes her own No. 1 out on its curl of receipt paper — the Lighthouse, the first night, before he knew there was any such thing as a tin — and lays it on her knee beside his No. 17, August next to February, and looks at the two of them together under the lamp. Then she puts them back where they go, hers at the bottom, his on top.

body: In half an hour it’s Lent, and he’s done with them, all forty days of it; and whatever gets counted after tonight is going to get counted knowing exactly what it’s for.
Lena puts her hand over the open tin, the way you’d cover a cup at a table so nobody fills it.
“It’s mine,” she says.

choices.key: On the levee you gave Lena back her tin with six new cigarettes in it, one for every fight since Christmas, each dated in your hand. You told her every one was her.
response: “Every one of them was you,” he says.
“I know,” she says. “I can read.”
But she doesn’t sound like she’s won anything. She puts the strips straight with one finger, every edge, and closes the lid down on them with both thumbs till it catches.

choices.text: “And four times I put it back.”
choices.key: On the levee you gave Lena back her tin with six new cigarettes in it, one for every fight since Christmas, each dated in your hand. You told her about the four you put back.
response: “And four times I put it back,” he says.

She waits for them, so he tells her the four. The Hollis back steps, the Monday of Dido, with the pack open in his hand. The Delgado front steps two days after that. The east stairwell at the end of January, the same stairwell as No. 13, the other way round. The far end of the Anacapa lot the night before the drive, in the dark past the last light, with the Odyssey sitting there packed.
She listens to all four with her hand on the lid.
“Then that’s four I’d have taken off you,” she says, and shuts it.

choices.key: On the levee you gave Lena back her tin with six new cigarettes in it, one for every fight since Christmas, each dated in your hand. You reminded her she’d said she would know.
response: “You said you’d know,” he says.

“I *would* have known.” She snaps the lid shut on it with one thumb, a sound like a latch. “I’d have known in January. I’d have smelled it on you across a seminar table, Costigan, I just wasn’t speaking to you.”

choices.key: On the levee you gave Lena back her tin with six new cigarettes in it, one for every fight since Christmas, each dated in your hand. You let her read them all.
response: He doesn’t say anything. He keeps his arm where it is and lets her.

response.text: She reads all seventeen, hers too — from No. 1 on the Lighthouse receipt paper down through the year to No. 17 under the air pump in El Paso — lifting each one and laying it back, and when she has read the last of them she shuts it.
response.else: She reads all eleven, every slip in her own capitals, from No. 1 on the Lighthouse receipt paper on, lifting each one and laying it back, and when she has read the last of them she shuts it.

s12k.slug: TUESDAY · 11:38 PM · THE MOONWALK — NOBODY’S OTHER ANYTHING
body: She puts the tin in the chest pocket of her jean jacket, the one that’s too small for anything, and it goes in, just, and she buttons the flap down over it.

His legs have turned to wood on the step. They get up without letting go of each other, which is worse than getting down was: she stands first, still inside the coat, and pulls, and he comes up off the wet boards with his knees cracking like Tony’s, and she says “Lord,” to his knees. Then they’re standing at the top of the steps under the lamp, as they stood at the rail two hours ago, her inside his open Carhartt, facing him, the fog coming up the steps behind her, her palms on his chest.

Down on Decatur the crowd has turned and is moving the other way now, up toward Bourbon, toward the horses: feathers and garbage-bag capes and a man carrying a cardboard pirogue over his head, a girl in a tiara on somebody’s shoulders with a go-cup in each hand. Somebody is blowing a whistle in the rhythm of the Who Dat. It’s twenty minutes to Lent, and the city knows it.
“So,” she says.
“So.”
“I’m not starting this as anybody’s other anything.” She says it to his face, every word. “Not yours, not hers, not his.”

“I spent two months being somebody’s girlfriend while I was out on my mama’s back steps being — whatever I was on those steps.” Her fingers spread on his shirt. “I won’t do that to anybody again. I won’t do it to *you*.”
“Me neither,” he says. “I’ve had a phone ringing in this pocket and your tin in the same pocket since Christmas.” Her fingers stop on his shirt. “Nobody’s other anything.”
“Sunday.” Her palms press. “I told you. After Mass. To his face, when we’re both back. The card, and whatever he wants to say to me after it, and he’s allowed all of it.”
“He’s going to be kind about it,” she says. “That’s what I can’t stand. He’s going to be kind to me about it, and I’m going to have to sit there and let him.”
“Tuesday,” he says. “When she’s back from Vancouver.”

He tries to see Tuesday and can’t. All he can see is her listening — the way she listens when it’s real, all of her turned toward it like a plant toward a window — and him having to keep on talking into that.

body.text: “I promised her. To her face.”
body.else: “To her face. That’s the least of it.”

body: “Tell her everything.”
“I’m going to.”
“Tell her about tonight. Tell her nothing happened.”
“Nothing did.”
“Tell her anyway,” Lena says. “I would want it said.”
“She ought to get it from somebody who isn’t standing on a levee with you inside his coat.”
“Then I’d better get out of your coat,” Lena says, and doesn’t. “By Tuesday night.”
“By Tuesday night.”
“And till then, nothing. Nothing either one of us would have to explain. Not to them. Not to Mama. Not in a confessional.”
“Nothing.”
“And you don’t kiss me.”
“I know.”
“I’m not telling you,” she says. “I’m telling me.”
“You’re very persuasive.”
“I’m going to be a lawyer, Jack. I practice on myself.”
“Then stop looking at my mouth.”
“I’m not.”
“You are. You have been since the rail.”
“So have you.”
“I’m allowed,” Lena says. “I’m from here.” But her eyes come up off his mouth to his eyes, which is harder.
What comes after Tuesday doesn’t get said. There’ll be a Wednesday; that’s as far as he can see from the top of these steps, and it’s far enough.
“What are you giving up?” she says. “For Lent.”
“Cigarettes.”
“…I know.” Her hand comes off his chest and goes to the flap of her pocket, over the tin, and rests there.
“You?”
“Something Laney’s going to take personally.”
“Coffee?”
“I’m giving something up, Jack. I’m not *dying*.”

And that’s the last of it. There’s nothing left on the levee to say tonight that isn’t the one thing they’ve just agreed not to. She doesn’t say anything. He doesn’t. The band on Decatur goes into something slow. Her hand comes back to his chest. The fog goes on climbing the steps. He could stand here till the trucks come.
She takes her hands off his chest.

It happens slowly enough that he feels every part of it: the heel of each hand, then the palms, then the fingertips last, and where they were the cold comes straight in through the flannel. She steps back out of his coat. One step. The Carhartt comes off her shoulders and swings back against his own, empty, and all the warm that has been in it for two hours goes out the front of him at once, into the fog, the way heat goes out of a kitchen when somebody opens the back door in January. The tin goes with her, in her pocket, the hard corner of it gone from his chest. And she takes another step.

His coat hangs open on nothing. His arms are still a little out from his sides, the shape of her. He wants her back inside it so badly it’s like a hand on the back of his neck, pushing. He doesn’t move. *Hail Mary,* he thinks, *full of grace,* and gets no further than that, and it’s enough to keep his boots where they are on the wet boards.
“That’s me, Jack,” she says, and there’s nothing on it at all — no drawl, no dare, none of the courtroom, none of the kitchen. “Pulling away. Watch me do it.”

He watches her do it. She doesn’t go anywhere. She stands two steps off at the top of the levee with her arms crossed tight over the pocket with the tin in it, shaking a little, and she waits for him.

choices.key: At the end of it, on the levee, Lena was the one who pulled away. You let her, and zipped up your coat.
response: He lets her. He brings the two sides of the Carhartt together and gets the zipper started, which takes three tries with his fingers stupid from the cold, and runs it up slowly, tooth by tooth, all the way to his chin.
She watches it go every inch of the way.
When he gets to the top she uncrosses her arms, and they go down off the Moonwalk together, side by side and apart on purpose, toward the white cathedral and the roaring.

choices.key: At the end of it, on the levee, Lena was the one who pulled away. “Sunday,” you said. “And then Tuesday,” she said.
response: “Sunday,” he says.
“Sunday,” she says. “And then Tuesday.”

That’s all. She turns toward the steps down to Decatur, and he comes up level with her, and they go down off the levee side by side with the cold kept where she put it, toward the Quarter, and he leaves it there.

choices.key: At the end of it, on the levee, Lena was the one who pulled away. You told her Lent was in eighteen minutes, and she told you to walk her to it.
response: “Lent’s in eighteen minutes,” he says.
Something happens at the corner of her mouth that she puts away again. “Then walk me to it, Youngstown.”

He walks her to it. Down the steps off the Moonwalk and across Decatur between the barricades, the two of them level with each other and nothing touching, deliberate as an altar boy and an altar girl going up the aisle with the candles.

s13.slug: TUESDAY · 11:52 PM · BOURBON STREET AT ST. ANN — THE HORSES
body: They walk up St. Ann from the square, past the dark mule stalls and the shut shops on Chartres and the lit galleries on Royal, side by side, a hand’s width apart, on purpose. Every block it gets louder. Every block he could close it, and every block he doesn’t, and she doesn’t, and the not-closing it is the hardest walking he has ever done.

Bourbon Street at eight minutes to midnight is the last of everything at once. It’s packed curb to curb and lit pink and green and gold from the bars, and the asphalt is shining wet with every kind of liquid and paved with beads, a crust of them, cracking underfoot. Up on a balcony a speaker is playing “TiK ToK” down at the street at full volume, and the people on the balcony are throwing the last of everything they have down into the crowd: beads, a stuffed alligator, a shoe. A man in a Superman cape and a Saints helmet is asleep standing up against a lamppost with a go-cup still level in his hand.

The others are on the corner where Luc told them to be. Theo and Laney each have a Lucky Dog in its paper, a bite out of each, going cold. Laney has the coconut held against her chest with her other arm, high up, like a heart she’s afraid she’ll drop. Margot is beside her with her hands in her coat. Kevin has his in his windbreaker, the right one around Theo’s phone. And Remy, found, somehow, in a purple Afro wig he can’t account for, is telling Margot about Frenchmen Street in a voice that suggests Frenchmen Street did something to him.

Laney sees them first. She reads Lena’s face, and then Jack’s, and gets nothing off either, and her mouth opens and shuts. Theo has gone very still. He looks at Jack about as long as it takes to read a page, and gets nothing either, and then he looks away down Bourbon at the lights.
“We got y’all a Lucky Dog,” Laney says, holding hers out.
“Nobody wants a Lucky Dog, Laney,” says Lena, and takes the place on the curb next to her, and Jack takes the place next to Lena. The space comes with them.
Then the street changes.

It starts where Luc said it would. First a pressure in the crowd up the block, toward Canal, before there’s anything to see, a whistle and the bars’ music cut off one door at a time and people turning to look. And then over the heads, high up, the horses: mounted police, forming a line across Bourbon from one curb to the other, and then coming down the street at a walk. They’re enormous up close. They blow white into the cold, and their shoes ring on the wet asphalt through the beads, and the riders sit up there in the dark blue and say nothing to anybody. They don’t need to. The crowd goes ahead of them, slowly, unhurried and complaining, like water ahead of a broom. Somebody near the corner yells “Mardi Gras is *over*!” and half the street cheers and the other half boos, and the balcony speaker cuts off in the middle of the chorus.

Behind the horses come the trucks: the street sweepers with their round brushes going, and behind them the water trucks, wetting it all down, beads and cups and the shoe, washing Mardi Gras into the gutters in one long gray roll. The smell of it comes ahead of them, wet pavement and diesel and soap.

On foot behind the horses, in the line, in the dark blue with his cap square on his head, is Luc. He sees his sister on the curb. He takes two fingers off his belt, and that’s hello. And then he sees who she’s standing next to, and the space between them, and he looks at that for the length of three steps, and nothing on his face moves at all, and he walks on behind the horses.
“Ritual closure,” Margot says, watching the line go by. “Enforced by livestock.”
Kevin takes his right hand out of his windbreaker. Theo is looking at his own watch, and the second hand is coming up on the twelve. Kevin holds the phone out to him.
“Lent,” Kevin says.
Theo takes it. “What do I give up?”
“You already did.”
Theo turns the phone on. It lights in his hand and plays its little music, and he holds it, and doesn’t look at it.
Somewhere toward the river a bell starts, and he loses count of it under the trucks.

The horses go on down Bourbon toward the Marigny end, and the brushes after them, and the water trucks after the brushes, and where they’ve been the street is suddenly a street: black and wet and shining under the bar lights, a few beads in the gutter the brushes missed, people going home in costumes they look embarrassed by now. A man picks up his shoe. It’s Lent. Lena stands beside him on the curb, not touching him, close enough that he can feel the cold she’s keeping on purpose, and the last thing Mardi Gras leaves him is that: the space between their hands, kept.

s13a.slug: WEDNESDAY · 12:08 AM · ESPLANADE AVENUE AT DECATUR
body: They walk out of the Quarter, the seven of them strung out along the sidewalk, not saying much, with the trucks grinding away behind them on Bourbon. Remy goes out front jingling his mother’s keys over his head like a sleigh bell. Laney carries the coconut in both arms. Margot walks beside her with her collar up. Kevin walks with his hands in his empty pockets, and Theo beside him carries his phone, still lit, still not looked at. At Esplanade the Mint stands lit at the river end, and the oaks start, reaching over the avenue from both sides with beads up in them, purple and green and gold, years of them, a strand stirring now and then when the air does.
Lena walks on the inside, by the iron fences, with her hands in her pockets and one of them over the flap with the tin under it.
The RAZR goes off in the breast pocket of the Carhartt, over his heart, alone in there now, against the place the tin was.

body: He can see her sending it: between takes, wet through, a towel around the robe and the forty pins, a truck idling somewhere that rains on cue, the white phone held up out of the wet in both hands. *i looked it up.* She would have. She doesn’t ask a thing till she’s read up on it, and then she asks the real one. Tuesday he’s going to tell her all of it, to her face.
He stops under a streetlight. The others go on ahead in their string under the oaks. Lena goes on a step past him and stops too, with her back to him, the fog in her hair, and doesn’t turn around.
“Answer her, Jack,” she says.

s13b.slug: WEDNESDAY · 12:12 AM · ESPLANADE AVENUE, UNDER THE OAKS
body: He shuts the phone and puts it back over his heart.

Lena starts walking again, and he catches her up in four steps and falls in beside her, and leaves the space where it is. The oaks go over them, block after block, with the old beads hanging in the branches, and a streetlight, and dark, and a streetlight. Behind them, toward the river, the trucks are still at it, a long way off now, and the city is quieter than he has ever heard it, and it’s Wednesday.

body.text: For a step or two the card from the vestibule at Holy Rosary is there behind his eyes, white in its frame — CONFESSIONS · SATURDAY · 3:00–4:00 P.M. — and Saturday is gone, and the morning will have to do.

body: Up ahead at the curb Remy has his mother’s car started and the heater going on high as if it were his job, and the doors standing open, and the others climbing in, Laney first with the coconut, then Margot, then Kevin, Theo last, his phone dark in his hand now. Two miles up the avenue, past Broad, on Dupre Street, Celeste will have left the porch light on. Jack and Lena walk to the car under the oaks, not touching, not hurrying, carrying the space between them the whole way like something full to the brim.
